title: Construct Validity in Psychological Tests
extended_summary:
This paper is a classic theoretical treatment of construct validity in psychological testing. It addresses the problem of how psychological tests should be interpreted when no single external criterion fully captures the attribute of interest, and argues that validation must go beyond simple test-criterion correlations. The authors distinguish construct validity from predictive validity, concurrent validity, and content validity, and explain why construct validation is needed for many psychological traits and abilities.

The paper does not study a generative AI intervention, reading/literacy instruction, or any educational treatment. Instead, it develops a general framework for test validation using examples from anxiety, intelligence, personality, and other psychological constructs. The discussion emphasizes the use of multiple sources of evidence, including group differences, correlation matrices, factor analysis, internal structure, change-over studies, and process analyses.

The main conclusion is that construct validity is established through a nomological network linking test scores to theoretical constructs and observable outcomes, not by a single coefficient or one criterion measure. The authors stress that negative findings can be informative, that alternative interpretations must be considered, and that practical use of a test requires a strong empirical fit between predicted and observed relations. This is a methodological paper rather than an empirical intervention study.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive computer-based instructional system that provides individualized guidance, feedback, and practice based on learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a conceptual discussion of construct validity in psychological tests and does not study an AI tutoring tool; ITS is the closest relevant archetype only as a general category.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical paper about construct validity in psychological tests, not an empirical study of an AI tool. There is no direct evaluation design, no K-12 literacy intervention, and no outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects are reported because no AI tool is tested. As a result, there is no evidence of impact on reading or literacy outcomes.
